The paper derives accurate formulas for calculating thermal fluctuations in multilayer interferometric coatings, taking into account light propagation inside the coating.
The authors use a transmission line model to describe the interferometric coating, consisting of alternating quarter-wavelength layers with different refractive indices.
The paper calculates the reflected wave phase as a function of small displacements of the boundaries between the coating layers.
The main contribution to the coating Brownian noise spectrum comes from the fluctuation displacements of the odd-numbered layers.
The paper's explicit calculations of coating Brownian noise give a slightly lower value of the spectral density compared to previous approximate methods, by about 5-17%.
The Khalili etalon is a double-mirror design where some of the coating layers are displaced to the rear surface of the mirror, which can potentially reduce the contribution of coating Brownian noise.
The paper states that its formulas can be applied to analyze coatings with non-quarter-wavelength layer thicknesses, such as those proposed to reduce thermal noise.
The numerical calculations in the paper use parameters for a Ta2O5/SiO2 coating on a fused silica substrate, with 20 Ta2O5 layers, 19 SiO2 layers, and a half-wavelength SiO2 cap layer.
The paper uses the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem to relate the spectral density of coating Brownian noise to the dissipated power when forces are applied to the layer positions.
The paper's approach provides a more accurate calculation of thermal noise in multilayer coatings compared to previous methods that assumed perfect reflection from the front surface.
The authors derive formulas for the reflected wave phase that account for the light propagation and reflections within the multilayer coating.
The paper's analysis shows that the contribution of even-numbered layer displacements to the reflected wave phase is negligible compared to the odd-numbered layers.
The paper's results suggest that the Khalili etalon design may be effective in reducing the contribution of coating Brownian noise to the overall noise spectrum.
The paper's formulas can be applied to analyze the thermal noise of coatings with non-quarter-wavelength layer thicknesses, which may be useful for designing coatings with reduced thermal noise.
The paper's approach provides a more detailed and accurate treatment of the light propagation within the multilayer coating, which is important for understanding the thermal noise mechanisms.
